Raising for long cycles

By lowob · 12 August 2026 · 5-minute read · Strategy

Long-cycle companies raise against milestones, not time. Build a capital stack that mixes dilutive, non-dilutive, strategic and project money, and show investors one retired risk per round.

This is commercial advice about how to run a raise, not investment advice.

Why the standard round does not fit

Part 3 said raise against evidence, not narrative. Part 4 said run the round like a sales process. Both hold. What changes in emerging tech is the clock.

A software company can close customers inside a twelve-month runway. A robotics, compute or energy company often cannot. The pilot alone may take a year. Procurement adds another. Revenue arrives after the money has gone.

So the round cannot be sized to time. It has to be sized to the next thing that makes the company worth more. That is a milestone, and the whole raise is built around naming it.

The capital stack for long cycles

No single source carries a long-cycle company. The stack is layered, and each layer has a job.

Source What it funds well What it costs
Milestone-based equity The next de-risking step Dilution, board seats
Grants and public funding Research, early prototypes, pilots in regulated sectors Reporting, slow timelines, restrictions on use
Strategic investors Capability the corporate needs Information rights, possible exclusivity pressure
Ecosystem and foundation funds Work that strengthens a shared protocol or network Alignment with the ecosystem's priorities
Project finance Proven assets with contracted cash flows Lender conditions, requires a proven model first

Non-dilutive money goes first where it exists. It is slow, and the reporting is real, but it funds the work investors will not pay for yet.

Strategic investors are useful when they need what you build. A corporate with a hard operational problem is a better partner than one running an innovation theatre. Check whether their ask is a cheque or a controlling relationship.

Project finance belongs later. It funds the hundredth unit, not the first. Using equity to build hardware that project finance could fund is a common and expensive mistake.

What investors want to see per milestone

Each round should retire one named risk. Investors in long-cycle companies look for three kinds of proof, roughly in order.

Technical de-risking: the thing works outside the lab, at the scale and conditions the customer needs. Not a demo. A deployment that survived a month.

A paying pilot: a customer with a budget put money against the problem. The amount matters less than the fact of payment. Free pilots are evidence of interest. Paid pilots are evidence of pain.

Regulatory clearance: for climate, energy, identity and anything near a utility or a government, permission is a milestone in itself. It is also a moat, because the next entrant has to earn it too.

Name the milestone this round funds. Name the one after it. An investor who can see two steps ahead will fund one.

Runway maths when sales cycles run twelve to twenty-four months

Start from the sales cycle, not from the burn. If the cycle is eighteen months, the first paying customer closes eighteen months after first contact, at best. Pipeline built today pays in the round after next.

That means the current round must fund the company through the whole cycle, plus the time to raise again. Eighteen months of cycle plus six months of raise is two years of runway, minimum. Most founders raise for twelve.

Three practical rules. Model revenue starting at month eighteen, not month six. Model pilots as cost, not income, until they convert. Model the next raise as a six-month project that starts when the milestone lands, not when the cash runs out.

Part 10 said build it to run without you. Here that includes a finance function that tracks milestone progress against cash, monthly, so the raise starts on time.

Narrative discipline: two slides

The deck has one job on slide one and a different job on slide two.

Slide one is the category. Why it will exist, why now, why it is large. This is where the investor decides whether to care.

Slide two is the next eighteen months. The milestone this round funds, the proof you will have, and what that proof makes possible. This is where the investor decides whether to write a cheque.

Most emerging tech decks are all slide one. They sell the future and never show the step. Investors who have seen a hundred category stories want to know what changes by next year.

Keep the claims register from Part 2 beside the deck. Every number on slide two should trace to a line in it.

The checklist

This round is sized to a named milestone, with the following milestone also named.

Non-dilutive sources have been mapped and applied for where they fit.

Strategic investors on the list need the capability, not a story for their board.

Runway covers the full sales cycle plus six months to raise again.

Revenue is modelled from the cycle length, and pilots are modelled as cost until converted.

Slide one is the category; slide two is the next eighteen months' proof.

lowob takeaways

  • Size each round to the next milestone that makes the company worth more, and name the one after it.
  • Investors look for technical de-risking, a paying pilot, and regulatory clearance, roughly in that order.
  • Slide one sells the category; slide two shows the next eighteen months' milestone and proof.
